result: PQ feeding induces dose-dependent lethality in adult Drosophila without causing gut leakage. The authors established that 15 mM PQ causes ~28% mortality after 18 hours and was chosen for further experiments, while gut leakage assays showed no treatment-related differences across PQ concentrations.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the PQ dosing model or gut leakage findings. The editor notes that 'experiments linking oxidative stress to DNA damage and energy expenditure are solid,' implicitly accepting the experimental setup and these foundational observations.

result: PQ treatment induces metabolic changes including upregulation of carbohydrate metabolism genes (InR, Pepck, Thor), activation of foxo-target genes, and depletion of stored glycogen and triglycerides, while free glucose levels remain unchanged. Fat body histology shows shrinkage of cell size and lipid-filled vesicles.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. One reviewer states 'experiments linking oxidative stress to DNA damage and energy expenditure are solid,' and another notes 'The authors demonstrate that hemocytes play an important role in energy mobilization during oxidative stress.' The metabolic phenotypes are accepted without critique.

result: Hemocytes are essential for oxidative stress response and energy mobilization. Hemocyte-deficient flies show significantly higher mortality on PQ (43% vs 13%), impaired triglyceride mobilization, and decreased free glucose levels, while hemocyte numbers remain unchanged by PQ treatment. The presence or absence of hemocytes determines susceptibility to oxidative stress.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this finding. One states 'They found that hemocytes are essential in this response' and 'The authors demonstrate that hemocytes play an important role in energy mobilization during oxidative stress.' Another reviewer emphasizes this as a key strength: 'The finding of stress-responsive immune cells capable of influencing whole-body metabolism adds insights.'

result: Single-nucleus RNA-seq identified 20 distinct cell clusters from 11,839 nuclei, including 8 hemocyte subclusters (7 plasmatocyte clusters and 1 crystal cell cluster). Hemocyte clusters show differential enrichment between control and PQ-treated conditions, with clusters C1 and C7 primarily from control flies, clusters C2-C4 and C6 predominantly from PQ-treated flies, and clusters C5 and C8 present in both conditions.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise this work. One states 'The identification of this distinct hemocyte subpopulation through single-cell RNA sequencing analysis and the finding of hemocytes that respond to oxidative stress are important. The method for single-cell RNA sequencing and related analyses are convincing.' Another notes 'using state-of-the-art single-cell transcriptomics, they identified expression changes at the level of individual hemocytes...which certainly represents very valuable work.'

result: Distinct plasmatocyte clusters show specialized transcriptional profiles. Control-enriched cluster C1 expresses hemocyte markers (Hml, Pxn), migration genes (Sema2a, Sema5c), and metabolic regulators. PQ-enriched clusters C2-C3 show metabolic adaptation signatures (Glut4EF, Lpin, bmm, Atg17, LpR1) indicating energy mobilization. Cluster C6, predominantly from PQ-treated flies, exhibits the most profound changes with strong immune activation (Jak/STAT targets Fas3, TotM), oxidative stress response (Hsp23/26/27), and cytoskeletal gene expression.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings as a key strength. One reviewer states 'The single cell analyses provide a clear description of how oxidative stress can cause distinct transcriptional changes in different populations of hemocytes.' Another notes 'One of the clusters appears to respond directly to oxidative stress and shows a very specific expression response that could be related to the observed systemic metabolic changes.'

result: In vitro PQ treatment of S2 cells recapitulates key features of cluster C6 plasmatocytes, showing dose-dependent increases in ROS and DNA damage, along with induction of Jak/STAT and JNK target genes. This supports that cluster C6 represents plasmatocytes directly responding to oxidative stress in vivo.
evaluation: Reviewers do not critique the S2 cell validation experiments. The overall acceptance of the cluster C6 characterization and the statement that 'experiments linking oxidative stress to DNA damage and energy expenditure are solid' implicitly supports these in vitro findings that validate the in vivo observations.

result: Cluster C6 shows enriched expression of Jak/STAT target genes (upd3, Socs36E, TotA, TotM, Fas3) with unique expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine upd3 not detected in other hemocyte clusters. Gadd45, linking DNA damage and JNK signaling, is also enriched in C6. These findings support that C6 represents activated plasmatocytes responding to oxidative stress through JNK and Jak/STAT pathways, with upd3 as a potential key mediator.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding as a major discovery. One states 'The discovery that DDR genes are required upon oxidative stress to modulate upd3 cytokine production and lethality provides interesting new insight.' Another notes 'the authors convincingly show that the DNA damage response in hemocytes regulates JNK activity and subsequent expression of the JAK/STAT ligand Upd3.'

result: Fat body snRNA-seq reveals 8 distinct clusters with differential enrichment by treatment condition. Control-enriched clusters (C1, C6, C8) show triglyceride storage gene expression, while PQ-enriched clusters (C2-C5) show oxidative stress response, Jak/STAT pathway activation (Socs36E, upd3, Fas3, TotA), JNK activation (puc, kay), and reduced triglyceride storage genes. Cluster C8, expressing AMPs, disappears after PQ treatment.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the fat body analysis without critique. The comprehensive acceptance of the single-cell approach and the statement that experiments are 'solid' and 'convincing' extends to the fat body findings, which complement the hemocyte data in demonstrating systemic responses to oxidative stress.

result: DDR-deficient flies (knockdown of mei-41, tefu, nbs) show significantly increased susceptibility to PQ (20-48% mortality vs 11% in controls) without effects on normal lifespan or starvation survival. Temperature-inducible adult-specific knockdown confirms these results. The increased susceptibility is not due to loss of hemocyte numbers or substantial DNA damage, but rather to altered DDR signaling modulating immune activation.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this finding. One states 'the authors convincingly show that the DNA damage response in hemocytes regulates JNK activity and subsequent expression of the JAK/STAT ligand Upd3.' Another notes this demonstrates 'the importance of tight control of JNK-Upd3 signaling in hemocytes during oxidative stress.' The use of multiple DDR genes and temporal control is implicitly accepted.

result: Loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes induces significant upregulation of upd3 and puc (JNK target) upon PQ treatment, along with dysregulation of metabolic genes (Thor, InR). Triglyceride mobilization remains efficient. DNA damage signaling in hemocytes essentially determines susceptibility to oxidative stress by modulating immune activation through JNK and upd3.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this mechanistic finding. One states 'Silencing of the DNA damage response or excessive activation of JNK and Upd3 leads to increased susceptibility to oxidative stress. This nicely demonstrates the importance of tight control of JNK-Upd3 signaling in hemocytes during oxidative stress.' The connection between DDR, JNK, and upd3 is accepted as convincing.

result: Hemocyte-specific upd3 overexpression drastically decreases survival on PQ, while upd3 knockdown has no effect. upd3-null mutants show reduced susceptibility to oxidative stress, but hemocyte-specific upd3 overexpression in the null background restores high susceptibility. Loss of upd3 rescues the increased susceptibility of DDR-deficient flies, confirming that DDR-regulated upd3 levels determine oxidative stress susceptibility.
evaluation: Reviewers support this genetic epistasis analysis. One notes 'the PQ-induced lethality seen when the DDR is disrupted can be rescued in upd3 null background, suggesting links between proper regulation of DDR in hemocytes, modulation of systemic upd3 signaling, and the control of oxidative stress survival.' The genetic rescue experiments are accepted as demonstrating the causal role of upd3.

result: JNK pathway manipulation shows that hemocyte-specific activation of JNK (hep[act]) increases susceptibility to PQ and induces upd3 expression, while dominant-negative JNK (bsk-DN) has no effect. This supports a substantial role for JNK-mediated upd3 induction in hemocytes during oxidative stress.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the JNK pathway analysis as part of the overall mechanistic framework. One states 'the authors convincingly show that the DNA damage response in hemocytes regulates JNK activity and subsequent expression of the JAK/STAT ligand Upd3,' which encompasses these JNK manipulation experiments. The pathway connection is treated as well-established.

result: The study reveals a defined immune-responsive subset of plasmatocytes (cluster C6) during oxidative stress. Oxidative stress-mediated immune activation is regulated by DNA damage signaling in hemocytes, which controls JNK activation and subsequent upd3 expression. Loss of DNA damage signaling or over-induction of JNK/upd3 in hemocytes renders flies more susceptible to oxidative stress.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support these integrative conclusions. One states 'The discovery that DDR genes are required upon oxidative stress to modulate upd3 cytokine production and lethality provides interesting new insight into the DDR may play non-canonical roles in controlling organismal responses to stress.' Another notes 'In the revised manuscript, the authors provide additional evidence to support the role of DNA damage-modulated cytokine release by hemocytes during oxidative stress responses.'

result: The authors postulate that hemocyte-derived upd3 from cluster C6 controls energy mobilization and tissue wasting upon oxidative stress, potentially through effects on the fat body which shows Jak/STAT activation that could be triggered by hemocyte-released cytokines.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly notes a limitation: 'It is important to note here that the association of upd3 with the observed changes in energy metabolism has not been tested, and the subsequent tissue wasting allegedly caused by excessive upd3 as a cause of death remains an open question.' This indicates the mechanistic link between upd3 and metabolic changes is speculative rather than directly demonstrated.
